title: DeliverC: Teaching Pointers through GenAI-Powered Game-Based Learning
venue: Proceedings of the 57th ACM Technical Symposium on Computer Science Education (SIGCSE 2026)
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of teaching C pointers, a concept that many novice programmers struggle to understand because of its abstract connection to memory operations. The authors ask whether a generative AI-powered game-based learning environment can improve motivation, engagement, self-efficacy, and perceptions of learning while helping students practice pointer concepts. They also investigate how effective students perceive AI-generated feedback to be during gameplay.

The intervention studied is DeliverC, a Unity-based educational game that uses GPT-4o-mini/GPT-4-mini to generate pointer-related challenges, evaluate student-written C code, provide personalized hints, and translate correct code into in-game actions. The game represents pointer operations through a delivery-truck metaphor on a grid, with scaffolded levels covering pointer initialization, arrays and pointer arithmetic, void pointers, multiple indirection, and function pointers. The system is designed to provide adaptive, real-time support rather than static pre-authored tasks.

The pilot was deployed in a summer undergraduate programming course at Pennsylvania State University in the United States. The course enrolled 37 students, and 25 undergraduates chose to participate in the optional extra-credit activity. Students completed up to three levels aligned with course pacing, and the evaluation drew on gameplay logs, descriptive statistics, a 15-item post-activity Likert survey, and open-ended responses. This places the study in a single-course higher education classroom context with both quantitative and qualitative data.

The main conclusions are that DeliverC showed promise for engaging students and supporting understanding of pointers through scaffolded, interactive practice. Most participating students reported greater confidence, reflection, and practical understanding, and gameplay logs suggested that students who progressed may have made fewer mistakes over time. However, participation dropped substantially across levels, and some students found the AI-generated feedback vague or unclear. The authors conclude that GenAI-enhanced game-based learning has potential for systems programming education, but feedback quality and broader scalability require further refinement.

identified_tools.name: DeliverC
identified_tools.description: A GenAI-powered game-based learning platform for teaching C pointers that embeds an OpenAI GPT model to generate personalized pointer challenges, evaluate student-written C code, provide tailored feedback, and translate correct solutions into game actions.
identified_tools.use_case: Studied as an undergraduate programming education tool for learning C pointers through scaffolded game levels with AI-generated tasks and feedback.

findings.finding_summary: In a pilot deployment, 25 of 37 enrolled undergraduate students participated in DeliverC at Level 1, with participation dropping to 20 at Level 2 and 8 at Level 3. The paper reports that error rates/attempt patterns improved for students who reached later scaffolded levels: although tasks became harder, the average and median number of attempts decreased in Level 3 relative to Level 2, suggesting learning progress through earlier practice. No effect size was reported.
findings.measure: Gameplay log data: participation by level and number of task attempts across Levels 1–3

findings.finding_summary: Survey results indicate that constructs such as metacognition, application, and confidence building received the strongest support, with over 75% of 25 students responding Agree or Strongly Agree. The authors conclude that most students felt more confident and reflective after using DeliverC. No effect size was reported.
findings.measure: 15-item post-activity Likert survey covering motivation, self-efficacy, metacognition, and related constructs

findings.finding_summary: Students generally viewed AI-generated feedback as helpful for revising strategies, but feedback clarity was weaker than other surveyed constructs. The paper notes that Clarity of Feedback and Formative Feedback received lower agreement than other areas, and some students reported receiving unclear, vague, or confusing hints. No effect size was reported.
findings.measure: Survey items on feedback quality plus open-ended responses about AI-generated hints/feedback

findings.finding_summary: Open-ended responses were largely favorable: 19 of 25 responses (76%) were positive, 3 (12%) were neutral/unclear, and 3 (12%) were negative. Positive comments emphasized that the game made learning pointers more fun, hands-on, and easier to understand, while negative comments focused on confusing levels and insufficiently clear instructions or hints.
findings.measure: Open-ended post-activity survey responses on student experience and engagement

findings.finding_summary: The paper reports strong initial engagement with DeliverC, with 25 students choosing to participate in the optional extra-credit activity at Level 1. Authors interpret survey responses as showing that most students found the game more motivating than traditional practice, though participation declined as difficulty increased and because the activity was optional. No effect size was reported.
findings.measure: Participation rates and motivation-related post-survey responses

findings.finding_summary: The authors report that DeliverC helped students understand pointer concepts, supported reflective learning, and enabled students to apply prior knowledge in new challenges. These conclusions are based on descriptive gameplay patterns, Likert survey responses, and thematic analysis rather than objective pre/post achievement tests. No effect size was reported.
findings.measure: Self-reported learning progress and understanding from post-activity survey and qualitative comments

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI GPT-family large language model used to generate tasks, produce reference solutions, evaluate student code, provide personalized feedback, and translate code into executable game commands.
identified_tools.use_case: Embedded inside DeliverC as the GenAI engine (reported as GPT-4-mini/GPT-4o-mini) powering adaptive challenge generation and feedback during gameplay.

findings.finding_summary: As the LLM backend for DeliverC, ChatGPT-supported feedback and task generation were associated with students reporting improved understanding, reflection, and confidence, but some students also reported that AI-generated hints were unclear or vague. The paper does not isolate ChatGPT experimentally from the DeliverC system, so findings are indirect and descriptive. No effect size was reported.
findings.measure: Student perceptions of AI-generated hints/feedback within DeliverC

quality_tier_rationale: This is a pilot mixed-methods study with descriptive gameplay analytics, post-activity survey data, and qualitative responses, but no randomized or quasi-experimental comparison and no objective pre/post achievement test. Evidence is suggestive but methodologically limited.
impact_tier_rationale: Reported impacts are mostly positive but based on self-reports and descriptive trends without standardized effect sizes or controlled causal estimates. The paper shows promising but still unclear magnitude of impact, with some mixed evidence around feedback clarity.
